title: EGDF：欧洲工作室正把重心从「过度饱和」的移动市场转向 PC
content:
European studios are moving focus from ‘oversaturated’ mobile market to PC, says EGDF – Mobilegamer.biz
Skip to content
The European Games Developer Federation says EU labour laws haven’t done much to halt job cuts across the region – and that more and more mobile studios are shifting focus to PC as the app stores reach oversaturation.
In
a data digest earlier this month
, we reported EGDF’s latest figures, which put Europe’s games workforce at around 123,000 people across 8,700 studios. To see how those jobs have held up over the past few years, and how mobile studios have fared, we asked EGDF managing director Jari-Pekka Kaleva for more details.
EGDF doesn’t break down jobs by platform because so many European studios work across several at once; but Kaleva said that broadly, “more and more developers have moved their focus from mobile to PC as mobile markets are oversaturated”.
“It is clear that the importance of PC markets for European studios – and their ability to employ people – has definitely increased,” Kaleva said.
In Germany, the share of studios making mobile games fell from 51% in 2021 to 37% in 2024, according to EGDF’s
2021
and
2024
reports, while the share making PC games rose from 59% to 79%. In Finland, the share making mobile games dipped from 66% to 61%, and in the UK, the share of studios whose main platform is mobile fell from 36% to 33%.
Smaller mobile studios tend to be more agile than big ones, said Kaleva, and have been quicker to move away from mobile.
The number of people working for game developers and publishers in 2024, by country. Credit: EGDF
Most European countries have seen a little growth, stagnation or a slight decline in total games staff, Kaleva said, pointing out that in countries with smaller industries, “even the closure of one individual studio can have a big impact on employee numbers”.
France and the Netherlands have been hit hardest, Kaleva said, while Türkiye and the UK have held up best, which he puts down to their “huge talent base with excellent access to both public funding and private risk capital locally”.
EGDF figures show Türkiye’s games workforce grew 38%, from 10,777 in 2023 to 14,918 in 2024, while the UK’s rose 12%, from 25,419 to 28,516, based on data from TIGA.
Across the industry, EGDF’s latest report says 95,000 people worked in EU game development in 2024.
“Growth in the EU game industry talent base stalled,” the report says. “It is clear that the global game industry’s investment winter and consolidation have hit the European game industry, with layoffs and a decline in new open positions in the job market.”
“The share of studios developing for each platform in 2024, according to EGDF.
The report adds that the EU workforce may even have shrunk by 1-2%, although some countries, such as Finland, Italy and Czechia, continued to grow modestly.
In the US, the Entertainment Software Association’s economic impact reports put the number of people working in video game software, which covers developers, studios and publishers, at more than 75,000 in
2023
and around 63,000 in
2025
, although Kaleva notes that the figures “are not entirely comparable methodologically” with EGDF’s.
Kaleva says it’s also important to separate layoffs from the overall number of people working in games. “If people laid off stay in the industry, for example by finding a new job or by becoming entrepreneurs, the total employee numbers do not change,” he explained.
“The employee numbers only drop if people leave the industry after the layoffs…some European studios have been able to grow quickly due to layoffs softening the hit in 2023-2024.”
EGDF’s platform data for 2024, including Serbia, North Macedonia and the UK. Credit: EGDF
Moving to another sector is harder in Europe, so developers tend to stay in games, said Kaleva, who added that some laid off staff are launching their own studios, which could explain why the number of studios in the EU has grown.
The exodus of developers and studios from Russia and Belarus, along with war refugees from Ukraine, has also boosted the industries in Lithuania, Poland and Cyprus, as well as Türkiye and Serbia outside the EU.
Kaleva added that the “real game industry powerhouse” is in Asia, pointing to
Amir Satvat’s data
showing a 10% rise in available jobs in Asia Pacific, while Europe’s have “basically stayed flat”.
As for whether European labour laws have made large-scale layoffs less common than in the US, or just slower, Kaleva said it largely depends on how a company is structured. “In some corporate groups, different studios are fairly independent and, to survive in the global markets, more or less on their own,” Kaleva explained. “Some are more centralised, and each subsidiary is specialised in something and collaborates with other subsidiaries around the globe.”
“In the first model, studios are closed down if they are not profitable regardless of labour laws. In the second model, labour laws might have more impact, but even then the question is much more about how well the role of the subsidiary in the corporate group matches the new vision of the corporate group after the restructuring.”
“And definitely, European labour laws have not stopped layoffs from happening in Europe… and many European countries did not have big studios in the first place, so we have not seen big layoffs in those countries either,” he added.
